title: Places and existence
title_target: どこですか — Doko desu ka
goal: Ask where things are, say whether something is there or not, describe where one thing is relative to another, and ask a stranger for directions.
bekal: tell あります (things) from います (living beings)
give positions with うえ・した・なか・となり
use the particle に for where something is
ask for directions and understand the answer
tell は and が apart in sentences about existence

dialogs.title: 会話 1 — Looking for the restroom and the office
dialogs.intro: Ani is in this building for the first time. Notice how は and が alternate throughout the dialogue.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]。[トイレは|Toire wa] [どこですか|doko desu ka]。
lines.id: Excuse me. Where is the restroom?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [トイレは|Toire wa] [あそこです|asoko desu]。[エレベーターの|Erebētā no] [となりです|tonari desu]。
lines.id: The restroom is over there. Next to the elevator.
lines.literal: restroom — as-for — over-there — is. elevator — 's — next-to — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ありがとうございます|Arigatō gozaimasu]。[この|Kono] [ビルに|biru ni] [コンビニは|konbini wa] [ありますか|arimasu ka]。
lines.id: Thank you. Is there a convenience store in this building?
lines.literal: thank-you. this — building — in — convenience-store — as-for — exists — [question]

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、1[かいに|kai ni] [あります|arimasu]。[いりぐちの|Iriguchi no] [ちかくです|chikaku desu]。
lines.id: Yes, on the 1st floor. Near the entrance.
lines.literal: yes, 1 — floor — on — exists. entrance — 's — near — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ATMも|ATM mo] [ありますか|arimasu ka]。
lines.id: Is there an ATM too?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [ATMは|ATM wa] [コンビニの|konbini no] [なかに|naka ni] [あります|arimasu]。
lines.id: The ATM is inside the convenience store.
lines.literal: ATM — as-for — convenience-store — 's — inside — in — exists.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [じゃあ|Jā]、[じむしょは|jimusho wa]？
lines.id: And the office?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [じむしょは|Jimusho wa] 3[かいです|kai desu]。[かいだんの|Kaidan no] [うえに|ue ni] [あります|arimasu]。
lines.id: The office is on the 3rd floor. It's at the top of the stairs.
lines.literal: office — as-for — 3 — floor — is. stairs — 's — top — at — exists.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [いま|Ima] [だれか|dareka] [いますか|imasu ka]。
lines.id: Is anyone there now?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[やまださんが|Yamada-san ga] [います|imasu]。
lines.id: Yes, Mr. Yamada is there.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [たすかりました|Tasukarimashita]。[ありがとうございます|Arigatō gozaimasu]。
lines.id: You've saved me. Thank you very much.

notes: **あります for inanimate things, います for living beings.** English uses one “there is” for both, but Japanese draws the line from the start: ほんが**あります** (there's a book), ねこが**います** (there's a cat). Choosing wrong won't make you unintelligible, but it instantly marks you as a beginner.
**Plants take あります.** Although alive, plants don't “move on their own”. A car with someone driving it? Still あります. The real rule isn't “alive” but **moves by its own will**.

**に marks where something is.** 1かい**に**あります = it's **on** the 1st floor. Don't confuse it with で (Unit 6), which marks where an **action** happens — two particles that both translate as “in/at” and are the most often mixed up.
**だれか = someone** (anyone), different from だれ (who). Adding か to a question word turns it into “some-”: なにか (something), どこか (somewhere), いつか (sometime).
**かい (階) = floor.** 1かい = いっかい, 3かい = さんがい ⚠️ (not さんかい), なんがい = which floor. Another counter whose sound shifts — the same family as 300 and 1 minute.
**Konbini** (コンビニ) is a 24-hour convenience store, short for *convenience store*. In Japan the konbini is also where you withdraw cash, pay bills, print documents, and send parcels.

grammars.title: [あります|arimasu] and [います|imasu] — two ways to say “there is”
body: There are two basic patterns, and both are used just as often. What separates them is **what the conversation is about**:

head: Pattern
Example
Used when
rows: **place** に **thing** が あります
[つくえの|Tsukue no] [うえに|ue ni] [ほんが|hon ga] [あります|arimasu]。
Describing what **is in a place**. The place is the starting point.
**thing** は **place** に あります
[ほんは|Hon wa] [つくえの|tsukue no] [うえに|ue ni] [あります|arimasu]。
Describing **where a thing is**. The thing is the starting point.
[きょうしつに|Kyōshitsu ni] [せんせいが|sensei ga] [います|imasu]。
The same, but for living beings.

after: **Why [は|wa] in one sentence and [が|ga] in another?** A rule of thumb that rarely fails: **[は|wa] marks what's already known**, **[が|ga] marks new information**. [トイレは|Toire wa] (we both know which restroom) [どこですか|doko desu ka]. [きょうしつに|kyōshitsu ni] [せんせいが|sensei ga] (new information) [います|imasu].

**Answering a [どこ|doko] question** almost always uses [は|wa] for the thing: [トイレは|Toire wa] [あそこです|asoko desu]. If you're unsure between [は|wa] and [が|ga] in a sentence about existence, ask yourself: does the listener already know about this thing? If so, [は|wa].

grammars.title: Position words — all through [の|no]
body: Positions always use the pattern **[reference] [の|no] [position] [に|ni]**. The reference point comes first, just like the [の|no] pattern from Unit 2.

head: Position word
Reading
Meaning
Example
rows: [つくえの|tsukue no] [うえ|ue] — on the desk
[いすの|isu no] [した|shita] — under the chair
[かばんの|kaban no] [なか|naka] — inside the bag
[うちの|uchi no] [そと|soto] — outside the house
[えきの|eki no] [まえ|mae] — in front of the station
[ビルの|biru no] [うしろ|ushiro] — behind the building
[ぎんこうの|ginkō no] [となり|tonari] — next to the bank
[がっこうの|gakkō no] [ちかく|chikaku] — near the school
[Aと|A to] [Bの|B no] [あいだ|aida] — between A and B
[みちの|michi no] [みぎ|migi] — right side of the road
[みちの|michi no] [ひだり|hidari] — left side of the road

after: **[となり|tonari] vs [ちかく|chikaku]:** [となり|tonari] means right next to, and of the same kind (a shop next to a shop). [ちかく|chikaku] just means somewhere around there, not necessarily touching.
**A position can be a whole answer:** [どこですか|doko desu ka] → [えきのまえです|eki no mae desu]。 Complete even without [あります|arimasu].

dialogs.title: 会話 2 — Asking the way
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost looking for the post office. Notice that Japanese directions are often a chain of landmarks, not street names — the Japanese address system doesn't use street names.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]、[ゆうびんきょくは|yūbinkyoku wa] [どこですか|doko desu ka]。
lines.id: Excuse me, where is the post office?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [ゆうびんきょくですか|Yūbinkyoku desu ka]。[あの|Ano] [しんごうの|shingō no] [ちかくです|chikaku desu]。
lines.id: The post office? It's near that traffic light.
lines.literal: post-office — is — [question]. that — traffic-light — 's — near — is.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [この|Kono] [みちを|michi o] [まっすぐですか|massugu desu ka]。
lines.id: Straight along this road?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]。[しんごうを|Shingō o] [みぎに|migi ni] [まがってください|magatte kudasai]。
lines.id: Yes. Turn right at the traffic light.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [みぎですね|Migi desu ne]。[そのあとは|Sono ato wa]？
lines.id: Right, OK. And after that?
lines.literal: right — is — right. that — after — as-for?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [ぎんこうと|Ginkō to] [コンビニの|konbini no] [あいだに|aida ni] [あります|arimasu]。[しろい|Shiroi] [ビルです|biru desu]。
lines.id: It's between the bank and the convenience store. A white building.
lines.literal: bank — and — convenience-store — 's — between — in — exists. white — building — is.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [ここから|Koko kara] [とおいですか|tōi desu ka]。
lines.id: Is it far from here?

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [いいえ|Iie]、[ちかいです|chikai desu]。[あるいて|Aruite] 5[ふんぐらいです|fun gurai desu]。
lines.id: No, it's close. About 5 minutes on foot.
lines.literal: no, near — is. walking — 5 — minutes — about — is.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [わかりました|Wakarimashita]。[どうも|Dōmo] [ありがとうございます|arigatō gozaimasu]。
lines.id: Got it. Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: ひと:
lines.text: [いいえ|Iie]、[きをつけて|ki o tsukete]。
lines.id: Not at all. Take care.

notes: **Japan doesn't use street names in addresses.** An address goes district → block → building number, from largest to smallest — the reverse of a typical Western address. That's why directions always come as landmarks: traffic lights, convenience stores, banks.

**を with a verb of motion means “through / along”**, not an object: みち**を**まっすぐ (straight **along** the road), しんごう**を**まがる (turn **at** the traffic light). This use of を is different from “marking the object” and only appears with verbs of motion.
**まがってください = please turn.** This is the て-form + ください, the way to ask someone to **do** something — the companion of the ください you learned in Unit 3. Fully explained in Unit 10.
**ぐらい / くらい = about, roughly.** 5ふんぐらい = about 5 minutes. It goes **after** the amount. Don't confuse it with ごろ, used for points in time: 3じごろ = around 3 o'clock.
**あるいて = on foot.** Its partners: でんしゃで (by train), くるまで (by car), バスで (by bus) — using the particle で you already know from Unit 3.
**きをつけて = take care.** A very common goodbye, literally “attach your attention”.

grammars.title: Asking for and giving directions
body: These five questions are enough to find almost anything in a Japanese city, and the six phrases after them are enough to understand the answer.

head: What you ask
Sentence
rows: [すみません|Sumimasen]、～[は|wa] [どこですか|doko desu ka]。
[このへんに|Kono hen ni] ～[は|wa] [ありますか|arimasu ka]。
[ここから|Koko kara] [とおいですか|tōi desu ka]。
[なんぷん|Nanpun] [ぐらいですか|gurai desu ka]。

head: What you hear
What it means
rows: [みぎに|Migi ni] [まがってください|magatte kudasai]。
[ひだりに|Hidari ni] [まがってください|magatte kudasai]。
[つぎの|Tsugi no] [しんごうです|shingō desu]。

after: **If you don't understand the answer**, don't just nod. Say: **[すみません|sumimasen]、[もういちど|mō ichido] [ゆっくり|yukkuri] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。** Japanese people are almost always happy to repeat — and often end up walking you there.

grammars.title: Floors, and counting them
body: Japanese buildings number floors from 1 at ground level, as in American English (there's no British-style “ground floor”). Basement floors take the prefix [ちか|chika] ([地下|chika]).
after: **The same sound pattern again.** Compare minutes in Unit 4 and hundreds in Unit 3: the numbers 1, 3, 6, 8, 10 are always the troublemakers. Once you recognize the pattern, new counters stop feeling like random memorization.

blocks.text: Some places use Japanese words, others loanwords. If you can read katakana, you've already mastered half this list before memorizing it.

head: Japanese
Meaning
Japanese
Meaning
rows: [ゆうびんきょく|yūbinkyoku] 郵便局

blocks.title: False friends
items: **ビル** = building (from *building*), not beer. Beer is **ビール**, with a long vowel. One ー mark separates “building” from “beer” — and people really do mix them up.
**デパート** comes from *department store* — it never means a government department.
**マンション** comes from *mansion*, but means an **apartment / condo**, not a luxury house.
**スーパー** comes from *supermarket* — cut off in the middle, like most long loanwords.

blocks.text: The best practice for position words is describing the room you're in right now. Read this example, then swap in the things around you:

blocks.title: A complete example
items: [わたしの|Watashi no] [へやに|heya ni] [つくえが|tsukue ga] [あります|arimasu]。
[つくえの|Tsukue no] [うえに|ue ni] [パソコンと|pasokon to] [ほんが|hon ga] [あります|arimasu]。
[つくえの|Tsukue no] [したに|shita ni] [かばんが|kaban ga] [あります|arimasu]。
[まどの|Mado no] [ちかくに|chikaku ni] [ベッドが|beddo ga] [あります|arimasu].
[へやの|Heya no] [なかに|naka ni] [ねこが|neko ga] [います|imasu]。
In my room there's a desk. On the desk there's a laptop and books. Under the desk there's a bag. Near the window there's a bed. In the room there's a cat.

blocks.text: Look at the last sentence: the cat takes **います**, everything else **あります**. Keep switching between the two until the choice becomes automatic — this is the one part of the unit that really needs repetition.

wave: Review Unit 4 while using this unit: describe your schedule today together with the places — “at 9 at the office, at 12 in the cafeteria, at 6 back home”. Time and place are the two backbones of everyday sentences; practicing them together is far more useful than separately.
